flashcards.q: What does the GIL actually protect?
flashcards.a: CPython's internal data structures, most importantly the reference count field on every PyObject, from concurrent unsynchronized modification by multiple threads executing bytecode simultaneously.

flashcards.q: Does the GIL protect against all Python-level race conditions like x += 1 on shared state?
flashcards.a: No -- the GIL guarantees individual bytecode instructions are atomic relative to other threads, but a multi-instruction sequence like load-modify-store can still be interrupted between instructions. It protects CPython internals, not application logic.

flashcards.q: Why can't reference counting alone reclaim reference cycles, and what supplements it?
flashcards.a: Two objects referencing each other (directly or transitively) never reach refcount zero through ordinary dereferencing even with no external references. CPython's generational cyclic garbage collector (gc module) periodically scans for and breaks unreachable cycles.

flashcards.q: Explain the 3.11+ specializing adaptive interpreter with an example.
flashcards.a: A generic bytecode instruction (e.g. BINARY_OP) that observes stable operand types at a call site is rewritten in-place to a specialized, faster variant (BINARY_OP_ADD_INT) with an inline guard. If the guard later fails (a different type arrives), it de-specializes back to the generic path.

flashcards.q: Is the specializing adaptive interpreter the same as a JIT compiler?
flashcards.a: No -- it specializes bytecode instructions executed by the interpreter loop itself, with no native machine code generation. CPython only began shipping an experimental true JIT (copy-and-patch, built on this specialization data) starting in 3.13.

flashcards.q: Why does I/O-bound multi-threaded Python get real concurrency but CPU-bound doesn't?
flashcards.a: The GIL is explicitly released around blocking I/O calls, so another thread can run bytecode while one thread blocks. CPU-bound code never blocks, so the GIL stays continuously held, serializing execution with no parallelism.

flashcards.q: How does NumPy achieve real multi-threaded parallelism despite the GIL for CPU-bound work?
flashcards.a: Its C-level hot loops explicitly release the GIL during long-running native computation since they're not touching Python objects/CPython internals during that time, letting other Python threads run concurrently.

flashcards.q: What are the concrete performance and memory costs of the free-threaded build as of Python 3.14?
flashcards.a: Roughly 5-10% single-threaded slowdown (down from ~40% in 3.13's experimental phase) and roughly 15-20% higher memory usage, from biased reference counting overhead and per-object lock metadata.

flashcards.q: What mechanism does the free-threaded build use to make reference counting thread-safe without the GIL?
flashcards.a: Biased reference counting: a fast path for the common case where an object is touched only by its owning thread, falling back to a slower atomic/shared path for genuine cross-thread references.

flashcards.q: What is CPython's free-threading rollout plan (PEP 703/779)?
flashcards.a: 3.14: officially supported but optional (build tag 't'). ~2026-27: GIL becomes runtime-flag-controllable. ~2028-30: free-threading becomes the DEFAULT, with GIL still available as an opt-in fallback.

flashcards.q: Why does the CPython team's free-threading rollout span multiple years instead of switching immediately?
flashcards.a: The C-extension ecosystem has relied implicitly on the GIL for thread safety for decades without extension authors needing explicit synchronization; an abrupt switch would silently introduce data races and crashes fleet-wide. The phased plan gives maintainers years to audit and update.

flashcards.q: What's the minimum common header every PyObject carries?
flashcards.a: At minimum ob_refcnt (reference count) and ob_type (pointer to the type object). Variable-length container types (PyVarObject: list, tuple, str, int) additionally carry ob_size.

flashcards.q: How do subinterpreters (PEP 684, 3.12+) differ from both free-threading and multiprocessing?
flashcards.a: Each subinterpreter has its own GIL (true parallelism, unlike classic threading) and shares the OS process (no fork/pickling overhead, unlike multiprocessing), but doesn't share Python objects directly by default — communication goes through explicit restricted channels, closer to message-passing than shared-memory threading.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't CPython's RSS shrink proportionally after objects are freed?
flashcards.a: pymalloc manages small objects (<~512 bytes) in 256KB arenas; an arena can only be returned to the OS once every pool within it is completely empty, so one long-lived small object can pin an otherwise-empty arena resident even though CPython considers that memory free for reuse.

flashcards.q: How did the compact dict implementation (guaranteed ordering since 3.7) reduce memory instead of increasing it?
flashcards.a: It splits storage into a sparse array of small integer indices plus a dense, insertion-ordered array of the actual hash/key/value triples — indices are far smaller than full triples, shrinking the sparse portion by roughly 20-25% while adding an ordering guarantee as a side effect of the dense array being append-only.
